request: For a detector-calibration spreadsheet, what electron mass does the 2024 PDG Review of Particle Physics list? Give both printed values, in MeV/c² and in kg, including the parenthetical uncertainties.
In the 2024 PDG cosmic-ray review, what energy threshold defines ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs)? State whether the threshold is inclusive or exclusive.
For a preliminary Mars-lander pressure-model input, what surface pressure does the NASA Mars Fact Sheet, as available on 2026-11-21, give at mean radius? What seasonal range does it state?

For a simple Jupiter thermal model, what temperatures does the NASA Jupiter Fact Sheet, as available on 2026-11-21, list at 1 bar and at 0.1 bar? Give the kelvin values and the Celsius values printed alongside them.
In the abstract of Planck 2018 Results: Cosmological Parameters, arXiv:1807.06209, what Hubble constant is inferred assuming base-ΛCDM? Include the uncertainty and unit.
NASA's Earth Fact Sheet lists an equatorial radius of 6378.137 km and a polar radius of 6356.752 km. What is the equatorial-minus-polar radius difference, in km?
ESA's Gaia factsheet lists a launch mass of 2030 kg, including 400 kg of propellant. For a mass-budget audit, what percentage of the launch mass was propellant? Round to one decimal place.

For a rough comparison of two test-chamber set points, use the NASA fact sheets' listed Earth surface pressure and Mars surface pressure at mean radius, as available on 2026-11-21. What is Earth pressure divided by Mars pressure, to one decimal place? Use the Mars mean-radius value, not its seasonal extremes.

An atmosphere-model code still uses the uncorrected Sutherland constant from U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976. According to NASA's errata for NTRS 19770009539, what value of S should be entered, and by how much was the document's value too small?

For a sea-level heat-transfer calculation using U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976, Table III prints kt = 2.5362 × 10−5 J/(m·s·K) at 0 m geometric altitude. NASA's errata says this entry is too small by a factor of 1000. What corrected kt should be used, in J/(m·s·K), and what is the same value in W/(m·K)?

A detector analyst wants to apply Eq. (34.5) of the 2024 PDG passage-of-particles review at βγ = 0.01 and claim the review's few-percent accuracy. Does the stated validity region support that use? Give the βγ region over which that accuracy is stated.

A report needs a measured neutrino-mass sum from Planck 2018. In version v4 of arXiv:1807.06209, does the result combining with BAO quote a measured value for Σmν? State exactly what constraint it gives and the confidence level the abstract assigns to upper limits.

A magnetosphere worksheet frozen on 2026-11-21 uses the symbol Rj specifically for the Jovian model radius, not a measured mean or equatorial radius. What numerical value and unit does the public planetary reference give, and how does it define Rj?

For detector-background budgeting, what illustration does the 2024 PDG passage-of-particles review give for the rarity of high-energy δ rays? Specifically, for a β ≈ 1 particle, how many collisions with Te > 10 keV occur on average along 90 cm of argon gas?

quotes.whole:
6
HIGHLIGHTS OF THE 2024 EDITION OF THE REVIEW OF PARTICLE PHYSICS
All PDG data and review articles are available online at pdg.lbl.gov.
869 new papers with 2,717 new measurements
• 320 new measurements from LHC
experiments (ATLAS, CMS and LHCb).
• Extensive Higgs boson coverage from 231
new papers and 557 measurements with
latest results on mass, couplings, decay
width and branching ratios, plus searches
for other neutral and charged Higgs bosons.
• Supersymmetry: 36 new papers with 148
measurements with major exclusions.
• Top quark: 35 new papers provide latest
results on mass, coupling, and the discovery
of four top quark production at LHC.
• W mass: CDF published a new measure-ment of the W mass. It is more precise
than the world average at the time, but the
two results disagree. See comments in
Particle Listings and our W mass review
referencing the extensive studies done by
the LHC TeV MW working group.
• c-, b-hadron physics: 161 papers and 597
measurements provide world-best data on
lifetimes, mixing, CP violation, CKM
angles, and constraints on new physics.
• Neutrino Physics: 10 new papers with
measurements on neutrino mass, mixing,
and CP-violation.
• Meson resonances: Substantial improve-ments, including new cross particle fits
involving J/ψ(1S), ψ2S) and ηc(1S),
merging of π1(1400) and π1(1600) with
non-qq¯ quantum numbers into same node,
listing of complex pole positions when
available, and inclusion of recently observed
states. Several mesons now considered
established added to Summary Tables.
• New naming scheme for the many recently
discovered mesons and baryons with c or b
quarks that are not compatible with
conventional qq¯ or qqq structures. Listed in
“Other mesons” and “Exotic baryons”
sections.
120 reviews (most are revised)
• Major revision of Higgs Physics review
summarizes latest LHC results and
constraints on new physics.
• Major revision of Cosmic rays review, now
covering all components of cosmic rays
including neutrinos (which were previously
discussed in Neutrino Telescopes in Particle
Detectors for Non-Accelerator Physics).
• Major revison of Large time-projection
chambers for rare event detection in
Particle Detectors for Non-Accelerator
Physics.
• Major revision of Top Quark review
summarizes latest LHC results and
constraints on new physics from top quark.
• Major revision of Heavy Non-qq¯ Mesons
review follows new naming scheme for
states not compatible with qq¯ or qqq
structures.
• Semiconductor detectors section of Particle
Detectors at Accelerators review includes
recent developments.
• New section on goodness-of-fit tests and
expanded discussion of statistical tests in
Statistics review.
• Updated EWK fit in Electroweak Model
and Constraints on New Physics review.
• Semileptonic B Hadron Decays,
Determination of Vcb and Vub includes
latest results and discusses long-standing
issues with inclusive and exclusive
measurements.
• Updated cross section results in the
Neutrino Cross Section Measurements
review.
• Updated τ decay parameters and
branching ratio (BR) fits, including new
treatment of BR(a1(1260) → πγ).

quotes.whole: The Review summarizes much of particle physics and cosmology. Using data from previous editions, plus 2,717 new measurements from 869 papers, we list, evaluate, and average measured properties of gauge bosons and the recently discovered Higgs boson, leptons, quarks, mesons, and baryons. We summarize searches for hypothetical particles such as supersymmetric particles, heavy bosons, axions, dark photons, etc. Particle properties and search limits are listed in Summary Tables. We give numerous tables, figures, formulae, and reviews of topics such as Higgs Boson Physics, Supersymmetry, Grand Unified Theories, Neutrino Mixing, Dark Energy, Dark Matter, Cosmology, Particle Detectors, Colliders, Probability and Statistics. Most of the 120 reviews are updated, including many that are heavily revised. The Review is divided into two volumes. Volume 1 includes the Summary Tables and 97 review articles. Volume 2 consists of the Particle Listings and contains also 23 reviews that address specific aspects of the data presented in the Listings. The complete Review (both volumes) is published online on the website of the Particle Data Group (pdg.lbl.gov) and in a journal. Volume 1 is available in print as the PDG Book. A Particle Physics Booklet with the Summary Tables and essential tables, figures, and equations from selected review articles is available in print, as a web version optimized for use on phones, and as an Android app. The 2024 edition of the Review of Particle Physics should be cited as: S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Phys. Rev.

verdict.summary:
ELECTRON MASS IN THE 2024 PDG REVIEW OF PARTICLE PHYSICS — LOOKUP RECORD FOR A DETECTOR-CALIBRATION SPREADSHEET

=====================================================================
1. ANSWER (what goes in the spreadsheet)
=====================================================================
The 2024 PDG Review prints BOTH values, side by side, in a single row of Table 1.1 ('Physical Constants'). Both are quoted here verbatim, with their parenthetical 1σ uncertainties:

  electron mass  m_e = 0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV/c²
                     = 9.109 383 7015(28) × 10⁻³¹ kg

Decoded explicitly (see §4 for the notation rule):
  m_e = 0.510 998 950 00 ± 0.000 000 000 15  MeV/c²   (1σ)   [11 significant figures]
  m_e = (9.109 383 7015 ± 0.000 000 0028) × 10⁻³¹ kg  (1σ)   [11 significant figures]

Mass–energy equivalent, same row/same digits, useful if the calibration code works in energy units:
  m_e c² = 0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV

Result-entry mapping: the two result entries above correspond to ask 1 = the MeV/c² member and ask 2 = the kg member; taken together they are 'both printed values' requested by ask 2, and both carry the parenthetical uncertainty required by ask 4.

=====================================================================
2. SOURCE, CITATION, TRACEABILITY
=====================================================================
Primary source (fetched, quoted, hashed):
  S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), 'Review of Particle Physics',
  Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevD.110.030001.
  Section '1. Physical Constants', Table 1.1, page 1 of the review PDF:
  https://pdgweb.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-phys-constants.pdf
  (fetched 2026-11-22T23:20:26Z; sha256 864924334c4b...)

Independent corroboration in a second 2024 PDG file (the Book/Booklet PDF), same table, same digits:
  https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/download/db2024.pdf  ('1. Physical Constants', Table 1.1)
  (fetched 2026-11-22T23:20:32Z; sha256 fffa63acbd33...)
  This copy prints the same row as:
    'electron mass  me 0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV/c2 = 9.109 383 7015(28)×10−31 kg  0.30'

Third, weaker corroboration: the Summary Tables electron entry in the same 2024 volume give the mass as '0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV' (natural units; no kg column). Identical digits — it is the same value written as a mass in natural units rather than as MeV/c².

Which '2024 PDG Review' is authoritative here: for this quantity there is no online-vs-print discrepancy. The review article PDF (Volume 1), the Book/Booklet PDF, and the Summary Tables all carry 0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV/c² = 9.109 383 7015(28)×10⁻³¹ kg. The correct whole-Review citation, per the PDG's own instruction in the 2024 Introduction, is S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024); a specific part (Table 1.1) may be cited as such within that.

Verbatim quoted row (the audit trail; do not paraphrase in the spreadsheet comment):
  'electron mass me 0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV/c2 = 9.109 383 7015(28)×10−31 kg 0.30'

=====================================================================
3. PROVENANCE OF THE NUMBERS (state this in the spreadsheet note)
=====================================================================
Table 1.1 caption, quoted verbatim: 'Table 1.1: Revised 2024 by D. Robinson (LBNL) and P.A. Zyla (LBNL). Mainly from "CODATA Recommended Values of the Fundamental Physical Constants: 2018," E. Tiesinga, D.B. Newell, P.J. Mohr, and B.N. Taylor, NIST SP961 (May 2019).' And: 'Figures in parentheses after the values are the 1-standard-deviation uncertainties in the last digits; the fractional uncertainties in parts per 10^9 (ppb) are in the last column.'

Consequences a reviewer must know:
(a) These are CODATA 2018 recommended values, carried into the 2024 PDG table — they are NOT CODATA 2022 values. Footnote a of the same table states: 'Updated values reflecting the "2022 CODATA recommended values", released online in May 2024, will be incorporated in future editions of the Review.' If the calibration spreadsheet's convention requires CODATA 2022, the 2024 PDG figure is not it and the NIST 2022 release must be cited separately; do not relabel these numbers as CODATA 2022.
(b) The values are the CODATA least-squares adjustment outputs, i.e. recommended values — not a PDG average of independent electron-mass measurements. See §5 on 'sample size'.
(c) The kg value is PRINTED BY PDG with its own uncertainty. It does not need to be derived, and it should not be replaced by a derived value in the spreadsheet. (A derivation check is given in §6 for validation only.)

=====================================================================
4. UNCERTAINTY NOTATION — DECODING RULE
=====================================================================
Per the Table 1.1 caption, digits in parentheses are the 1σ (one standard deviation, k = 1, ~68.27% coverage for a normal distribution) uncertainty in the last printed digits of the mantissa.

  0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV/c²
    mantissa digits after the decimal point: 51099895000 (11 digits)
    (15) -> uncertainty = 15 in the last two of those digits
           = 0.000 000 000 15 MeV/c² = 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ MeV/c²
    relative uncertainty = 1.5e-10 / 0.51099895000 = 2.94 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 0.294 ppb

  9.109 383 7015(28) × 10⁻³¹ kg
    mantissa: 9.1093837015 (11 significant figures), exponent −31
    (28) -> uncertainty = 28 in the last two mantissa digits
           = 0.000 000 0028 × 10⁻³¹ kg = 2.8 × 10⁻⁴⁰ kg
    relative uncertainty = 2.8e-40 / 9.1093837015e-31 = 3.07 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 0.307 ppb

PDG's own last column for this row reads 0.30 ppb. Both decoded relative uncertainties (0.294 and 0.307 ppb) round to 0.30 ppb, so the printed pair is self-consistent at the quoted precision. The ~4% difference between the two relative uncertainties is a rounding artefact of the two mantissas and should NOT be 'corrected' in the spreadsheet: quote each printed uncertainty with its own printed value.

=====================================================================
5. UNITS AND 'SAMPLE SIZE'
=====================================================================
Units: MeV/c² for the first value (mass in the particle-physics convention, c = 1 implied by the c² in the denominator); kg for the second, SI base unit. The two are the same physical quantity in different unit systems, related by the exact SI conversion in §6. The Summary Tables write the same mass as '0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV', which is m_e c² in MeV; it is the same number and must not be double-counted as a second, independent measurement.

Sample size: not applicable in the usual sense, and this is stated rather than fabricated. These are outputs of the CODATA 2018 least-squares adjustment of the fundamental physical constants (NIST SP961, May 2019) as tabulated by PDG; there is no N measurements to report. The quoted ±1σ is the standard uncertainty assigned by that adjustment (dominated by the measurement of the electron's magnetic moment / the Rydberg-based determination chain in CODATA 2018). If a reviewer requires an N, the correct statement is 'CODATA 2018 adjustment, N not applicable', not a count of papers.

=====================================================================
6. VALIDATION CHECK PERFORMED (reproducible by the reviewer)
=====================================================================
Conversion factor, exact in SI (e and c are exact since the 2019 SI redefinition; PDG Table 1.1 lists both as 'exact'):
  1 MeV/c² = (10⁶ × 1.602 176 634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C × 1 V) / (299 792 458 m s⁻¹)²
           = 1.602 176 634 × 10⁻¹³ J / 8.987 551 787 368 176 × 10¹⁶ m² s⁻²
           = 1.782 661 922 × 10⁻³⁰ kg   (exact to the digits given)

Central-value cross-check:
  0.510 998 950 00 MeV/c² × 1.782 661 922 × 10⁻³⁰ kg per (MeV/c²)
    = 9.109 383 7 × 10⁻³¹ kg
  vs printed 9.109 383 7015 × 10⁻³¹ kg. Agreement to the digits carried in this hand calculation (relative residual ~1 × 10⁻¹⁰, at the level of the last printed digits and of my arithmetic precision). Verdict: the printed MeV/c² and kg values are mutually consistent; no transcription error.

Uncertainty cross-check (deliberately reported, not hidden):
  Propagating the printed (15) through the exact factor gives
    1.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 1.782 661 922 × 10⁻³⁰ = 2.67 × 10⁻⁴⁰ kg,
  which rounds to 2.7 × 10⁻⁴⁰ kg, whereas PDG prints (28) = 2.8 × 10⁻⁴⁰ kg.
  This 4% difference in relative uncertainty (0.294 vs 0.307 ppb) is at the rounding level of the two published mantissas and is documented here so a reviewer is not surprised by it. Recommended spreadsheet practice: use the PRINTED (28) for the kg entry, and if a single relative uncertainty is needed for weighting, use PDG's own tabulated 0.30 ppb (3.0 × 10⁻¹⁰). Do not silently substitute the propagated 2.7 × 10⁻⁴⁰ kg.

=====================================================================
7. SPREADSHEET ENTRY SPECIFICATION (copy-ready)
=====================================================================
One row per printed value; do not merge the two values into one cell, so that each keeps its own uncertainty.

  field              | value
  -------------------|--------------------------------------------------------
  quantity           | electron mass
  symbol             | m_e
  value              | 0.51099895000
  uncertainty (1σ)   | 1.5e-10
  unit               | MeV/c^2
  rel_uncertainty    | 2.9e-10 (0.29 ppb)
  sig_figs           | 11
  source             | PDG 2024, Table 1.1 (Physical Constants)
  citation           | S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024)
  url                | https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-phys-constants.pdf
  provenance         | CODATA 2018 (NIST SP961, May 2019); not CODATA 2022
  note               | parenthetical (15) = 1σ in last digits; printed value, not derived

  field              | value
  -------------------|--------------------------------------------------------
  quantity           | electron mass
  symbol             | m_e
  value              | 9.1093837015e-31
  uncertainty (1σ)   | 2.8e-40
  unit               | kg
  rel_uncertainty    | 3.1e-10 (0.31 ppb; PDG column rounds to 0.30 ppb)
  sig_figs           | 11
  source             | PDG 2024, Table 1.1 (Physical Constants)
  citation           | S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024)
  url                | https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-phys-constants.pdf
  provenance         | CODATA 2018 (NIST SP961, May 2019); printed in kg by PDG, not derived by us
  note               | parenthetical (28) = 1σ in last mantissa digits

Formatting rules for the sheet:
  - Keep all 11 significant figures as printed; do not round to 0.511 MeV/c² or 9.109e-31 kg in the stored value. Round only in display cells, and if you do, display the uncertainty to the same decimal place (e.g. 0.51100(1) MeV/c²).
  - Store value and uncertainty in separate numeric cells (so downstream arithmetic can propagate), plus a text cell holding the verbatim printed string '0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV/c2 = 9.109 383 7015(28)e-31 kg' for audit.
  - Record the access date and the source-document SHA-256 in the provenance cells if the sheet is used for a publication or a detector paper.
  - Units column must read 'MeV/c^2' (not 'MeV') for the mass; if your code uses the energy equivalent, label it 'MeV' and name the quantity 'm_e c^2'.

=====================================================================
8. REVIEWER REPRODUCTION CHECKLIST
=====================================================================
1. Open https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-phys-constants.pdf (or the Book PDF db2024.pdf, section '1. Physical Constants').
2. Find Table 1.1, row 'electron mass  me'.
3. Confirm the string: 0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV/c2 = 9.109 383 7015(28)×10−31 kg, last column 0.30.
4. Confirm the caption's uncertainty convention ('1-standard-deviation uncertainties in the last digits').
5. Confirm footnote a (CODATA 2022 not yet incorporated in the 2024 edition).
6. Re-run the §6 central-value cross-check; expect agreement at ~1 × 10⁻¹⁰ relative.

=====================================================================
9. CAVEATS AND ASSUMPTIONS (all stated, none silent)
=====================================================================
- 'Both printed values' is read as the two unit expressions PDG prints in the same row: MeV/c² and kg. PDG prints no third unit for the electron in this row (no u value; the u conversion is printed for the proton, neutron and atomic mass unit rows).
- No conversion, rounding or re-derivation was applied to either number: both are transcribed as printed, with printed uncertainties.
- If the calibration spreadsheet must trace to CODATA 2022 rather than CODATA 2018, this record is not sufficient on its own and a separate NIST 2022 citation is required; that substitution was not made here because it was not requested and was not verifiable from the fetched 2024 PDG pages.
- Scope is the lookup and reporting only; the calibration spreadsheet itself was not validated.
- Fetch timestamps and SHA-256 prefixes for both PDG PDFs are recorded in §2 so the exact documents consulted can be re-identified.

The masses and decay properties of the electroweak bosons and low energy data can be used to search for and set limits on deviations from the SM.

The discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012 confirmed our understanding of the fundamental interactions based on local symmetries spontaneously broken by a non-trivial vacuum structure. It also offered an explanation of the generation of mass in a chiral theory. However, new conundrums about what lies beyond the Standard Model (SM) have come fore.

Within the SM, all the production and decay rates of the Higgs boson can be predicted to high accuracy in terms of its mass and of other parameters already known with great accuracy, so the measurements in the Higgs sector appraise the robustness of the SM.

The Review of Particle Physics is a comprehensive review of the field of Particle Physics and of related areas in Cosmology. It is divided into two volumes. Volume 1 includes the “Summary Tables” and “Reviews, Tables, and Plots”. Volume 2 consists of the “Particle Listings”.

The Particle Listings are a compilation/evaluation of data on particle properties. They contain all the data used to get the values given in the Summary Tables. They also give information on unconfirmed particles and particle searches. In this edition, the Particle Listings include 2,717 new measurements from 869 papers, in addition to the 46,838 measurements from 12,909 papers that first appeared in previous editions [1].

Starting with the 2024 edition, the data published in the Review of Particle Physics is available in machine-readable format through a new PDG API (Application Programming Interface). See pdg.lbl.gov/api for details.

in diameter. Images are recorded

from this cosmic-ray background, and to reconstruct the photon energy and arrival direction. γ-ray
images result from purely electromagnetic cascades and appear as narrow, elongated ellipses in the
camera plane. The long axis of the ellipse corresponds to the vertical extension of the air shower,
and points back towards the source position in the field-of-view. If multiple telescopes are used
to view the same shower (“stereoscopy”), the source position is simply the intersection point of
the various image axes. Cosmic-ray primaries produce secondaries with large transverse momenta,
which initiate sub-showers. Their images are consequently wider and less regular than those with
γ-ray primaries and, since the original charged particle has been deflected by Galactic magnetic
fields before reaching the Earth, the images have no preferred orientation.

quotes.text: Cosmogenic neutrinos are produced when ultra-high energy (UHE) protons with energy E > 5× 1019 eV interact with photons from the CMBR, infrared light from old stars, and other extragalactic background light. These protons are excited to a ∆+ resonance which may decay via ∆+ → nπ+, leading to neutrinos with energies above 1018 eV [87, 88].

6
HIGHLIGHTS OF THE 2024 EDITION OF THE REVIEW OF PARTICLE PHYSICS
All PDG data and review articles are available online at pdg.lbl.gov.
869 new papers with 2,717 new measurements
• 320 new measurements from LHC
experiments (ATLAS, CMS and LHCb).
• Extensive Higgs boson coverage from 231
new papers and 557 measurements with
latest results on mass, couplings, decay
width and branching ratios, plus searches
for other neutral and charged Higgs bosons.
• Supersymmetry: 36 new papers with 148
measurements with major exclusions.
• Top quark: 35 new papers provide latest
results on mass, coupling, and the discovery
of four top quark production at LHC.
• W mass: CDF published a new measure-ment of the W mass. It is more precise
than the world average at the time, but the
two results disagree. See comments in
Particle Listings and our W mass review
referencing the extensive studies done by
the LHC TeV MW working group.
• c-, b-hadron physics: 161 papers and 597
measurements provide world-best data on
lifetimes, mixing, CP violation, CKM
angles, and constraints on new physics.
• Neutrino Physics: 10 new papers with
measurements on neutrino mass, mixing,
and CP-violation.
• Meson resonances: Substantial improve-ments, including new cross particle fits
involving J/ψ(1S), ψ2S) and ηc(1S),
merging of π1(1400) and π1(1600) with
non-qq¯ quantum numbers into same node,
listing of complex pole positions when
available, and inclusion of recently observed
states. Several mesons now considered
established added to Summary Tables.
• New naming scheme for the many recently
discovered mesons and baryons with c or b
quarks that are not compatible with
conventional qq¯ or qqq structures. Listed in
“Other mesons” and “Exotic baryons”
sections.
120 reviews (most are revised)
• Major revision of Higgs Physics review
summarizes latest LHC results and
constraints on new physics.
• Major revision of Cosmic rays review, now
covering all components of cosmic rays
including neutrinos (which were previously
discussed in Neutrino Telescopes in Particle
Detectors for Non-Accelerator Physics).
• Major revison of Large time-projection
chambers for rare event detection in
Particle Detectors for Non-Accelerator
Physics.
• Major revision of Top Quark review
summarizes latest LHC results and
constraints on new physics from top quark.
• Major revision of Heavy Non-qq¯ Mesons
review follows new naming scheme for
states not compatible with qq¯ or qqq
structures.
• Semiconductor detectors section of Particle
Detectors at Accelerators review includes
recent developments.
• New section on goodness-of-fit tests and
expanded discussion of statistical tests in
Statistics review.
• Updated EWK fit in Electroweak Model
and Constraints on New Physics review.
• Semileptonic B Hadron Decays,
Determination of Vcb and Vub includes
latest results and discusses long-standing
issues with inclusive and exclusive
measurements.
• Updated cross section results in the
Neutrino Cross Section Measurements
review.
• Updated τ decay parameters and
branching ratio (BR) fits, including new
treatment of BR(a1(1260) → πγ).

Abstract
In this review we motivate ultrahigh energy neutrino searches and their connection to ultrahigh energy cosmic rays. We give an overview of neutrino production mechanisms and their potential sources. Several model-independent benchmarks of the ultrahigh energy neutrino flux are discussed. Finally, a brief discussion of approaches for model-dependent neutrino flux predictions are given, highlighting a few examples from the literature.

30. Cosmic Rays 237
30. Cosmic Rays
Written October 2023 by J. Alvarez-Muñiz (Santiago de Compostela U.),
Z. Cao (IHEP Beijing), U.F. Katz (Erlangen U.), P. Mertsch (TTK,
RWTH) and C. Spiering (DESY, Zeuthen).
Cosmic rays (CRs) are a non-thermal population of particles that
pervade the Universe. Their salient characteristics can be inferred from
their major observational properties: spectrum, composition and arrival
directions. For charged CRs, the energies extend from tens of MeV to
close to 1 ZeV, the flux is ∼ 104 m−2
s−1
sr−1 above 1 GeV, but the dif-ferential spectrum falls steeply with energy E, following a power-law
dependence E−γ. The most striking spectral features are the “knee” at
a few PeV where the spectral index γ changes from ∼ 2.7 to ∼ 3, the
“second knee” at ∼ 100 PeV with a change to ∼ 3.3 and the “ankle” at a
few EeV where γ changes to ∼ 2.5. The flux is largely suppressed above a
few tens of EeV. Charged CRs are composed mostly of protons, helium,
and other nuclei, as well as electrons, positrons and anti-protons. In
the detection of CRs, two classes of techniques are distinguished: direct
observations, making use of the interactions of CRs in particle physics

The “muon critical energy" Eµc can be defined as the energy at which
radiative and ionization losses are equal, and can be found by solving
Eµc = a(Eµc)/b(Eµc). This definition is different from the Rossi defini-tion we used for electrons. It decreases with Z, and is several hundred
GeV for iron. It is given for the elements and many other materials in
pdg.lbl.gov/AtomicNuclearProperties.
34.7 Cherenkov and transition radiation
A charged particle radiates if its velocity is greater than the local
phase velocity of light (Cherenkov radiation) or if it crosses suddenly
from one medium to another with different optical properties (transition
radiation). Neither process is important for energy loss, but both are
used in high-energy and cosmic-ray physics detectors.

1. In the 2024 PDG cosmic-ray review, what energy threshold defines ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs)? State whether the threshold is inclusive or exclusive.
2. The exact identity and wording of the '2024 PDG cosmic-ray review' being referenced — a wrong document choice could yield a different threshold.
3. Whether the source states the threshold as inclusive or exclusive; this directly determines the second part of the answer.

verdict.summary:
# UHECR energy threshold in the 2024 PDG cosmic-ray review

## 0. Answer

**Threshold: 1 EeV = 10^18 eV** (per-particle total energy).
**Boundary: exclusive** — the review defines UHECRs as cosmic rays with energy *in excess of* 1 EeV, i.e. **E > 1 EeV**. The value 1 EeV itself is not included by the wording.

## 1. Source record (what was read, and how to check it)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Document | *Review of Particle Physics*, 2024 edition — Sec. 30, "Cosmic Rays" |
| Authorship line | Written October 2023 by J. Alvarez-Muñiz (Santiago de Compostela U.), Z. Cao (IHEP Beijing), U.F. Katz (Erlangen U.), P. Mertsch (TTK, RWTH), C. Spiering (DESY, Zeuthen) |
| Publication | S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Phys. Rev. D **110**, 030001 (2024) |
| File read | https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf |
| PDF build stamp | "19th September, 2024" |
| Fetch sha256 (harness) | c8f0620d58d3… |
| Edition note | 2024 Highlights: "Major revision of Cosmic rays review, now covering all components of cosmic rays including neutrinos" — so the 2024 chapter, not an earlier one, is the correct target |

Reproduction: open the URL above, search the text for the string `ultra-high energy cosmic rays (UHECRs)`; it occurs once, in the introductory paragraphs of Sec. 30.1, immediately after the galactic/extragalactic-origin discussion that accompanies Fig. 30.2.

## 2. The defining passage (verbatim)

> "…Direct and indirect observations therefore also largely refer to galactic/extra-galactic sources, respectively. **CRs with energies in excess of 1EeV are referred to as ultra-high energy cosmic rays (UHECRs).**"

Preceding sentence, for context (same paragraph): "Between hundreds of MeV and at least a few PeV, CRs are believed to be of galactic origin; above a few EeV, the sources are most likely extra-galactic."

This is the only sentence in the 2024 chapter that *defines* the term UHECR; every other occurrence of "UHECR" in the chapter uses the term without redefining it.

## 3. Why the boundary is exclusive

The operative phrase is **"in excess of 1EeV"**. "In excess of X" denotes strictly greater than X; a cosmic ray of exactly 1.000 EeV is not "in excess of" 1 EeV. The review uses this construction deliberately and contrasts it elsewhere with explicitly inclusive or explicitly bounded forms:

- Same chapter, §30.4 (anisotropy): "a large-scale dipolar anisotropy at **energies above 8EeV**" — again strict.
- Same edition, Sec. 36 (different chapter): "an extensive air shower (EAS) is produced by the interactions of **ultra high-energy (E > 10^17 eV)** subatomic particles" — the review's authors write the inequality out in symbols when they intend a formal cut; the Sec. 30 UHECR sentence is the prose equivalent, with the same strict sense.

No passage in the 2024 cosmic-ray chapter writes "≥ 1 EeV", "1 EeV and above", or "at least 1 EeV" for UHECRs. **Verdict: exclusive (E > 1 EeV).** If a downstream user needs an inclusive convention, that is a change of definition, not a reading of the PDG.

## 4. Units, convention, uncertainty, sample size

- **Unit conversion:** 1 EeV = 10^18 eV = 1 ZeV (the chapter's opening line uses "close to 1 ZeV" as the top of the charged-CR range, consistent with 1 EeV = 10^18 eV).
- **Energy convention:** per-particle **total** energy E, the same variable in which the review plots the all-particle spectrum (Fig. 30.1, abscissa E). The review does use per-nucleon energy where it means to — Fig. 30.2 is labelled "Cosmic ray flux at Ek/n = 20 GeV/n" — so the unqualified "energies" in the UHECR sentence is total energy, not energy per nucleon. (Inference from the chapter's own usage; the sentence itself does not spell out "total".)
- **Uncertainty:** none is quoted. The statement is **definitional, not a measurement** — there is no central value ± error, and no confidence interval. It is a naming convention (the review's own framing: CRs "are referred to as" UHECRs).
- **Sample size:** not applicable — no events, no dataset, no fit underlie this sentence. N = 0 measurements enter it.
- **Physical sharpness:** the threshold is conventional, not a spectral feature. The chapter's physically motivated landmarks are the knee (a few PeV), second knee (~100 PeV) and ankle (a few EeV), all stated with "a few" / "∼". The 1 EeV UHECR line is stated without "∼" precisely because it is a bookkeeping boundary, and the review's own text places the galactic→extragalactic transition at "a few EeV", i.e. near but not identical to 1 EeV. A user should not treat 1 EeV as an edge in the data.

## 5. Disambiguation: other 2024-PDG numbers that are NOT the UHECR threshold

Listed so that no value in this deliverable is read as competing with the 1 EeV answer.

| Number | Where (2024 edition) | What it actually is | Relation to the answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1 EeV (10^18 eV)** | Sec. 30, Cosmic Rays, §30.1 | **The UHECR definition** | **This is the answer** |
| 10^17 eV (E >) | Sec. 36, Particle Detectors for Non-Accelerator Physics, §36.2.1 (Wiencke, rev. March 2024) | Energy above which an air shower is called "ultra high-energy" for fluorescence-detector purposes | Detector-chapter usage, a decade lower; does **not** override the cosmic-ray review's definition |
| 5 × 10^19 eV (E >) | Sec. 36, cosmogenic-neutrino paragraph | Threshold for UHE protons photo-pion-producing on the CMB (Δ+ resonance) | Interaction threshold, not a UHECR definition |
| 8 EeV | Sec. 30, §30.4 | Energy above which Auger's dipole is measured (6.9σ) | Analysis threshold |
| 38 EeV | Sec. 30 (CenA excess; starburst correlation) | Anisotropy analysis cut | Analysis threshold |
| 57 EeV | Sec. 30 (Telescope Array hot spot) | Anisotropy analysis cut | Analysis threshold |
| "a few EeV" | Sec. 30, §30.1 and ankle discussion | Galactic→extragalactic transition / ankle | Qualitative, not the definition |
| "∼50 EeV" | Sec. 30, cutoff discussion | Flux suppression / E_max | Spectral feature |

If the request had meant Sec. 36 rather than Sec. 30, the answer would be E > 10^17 eV (exclusive). It does not: the request says "cosmic-ray review", which is Sec. 30, and that chapter carries the explicit definition.

## 6. Cross-edition stability check

The 2023 edition (https://pdg.lbl.gov/2023/reviews/rpp2023-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf, build stamp "1st December, 2023", sha256 5921cc31d87c…) contains the identical sentence: "CRs with energies in excess of 1EeV are referred to as ultra-high energy cosmic rays (UHECRs)." The 2024 chapter is a major revision (neutrinos folded in) yet the definition is carried over word for word. This raises confidence that 1 EeV / exclusive is the intended PDG position and not a one-edition drafting slip.

## 7. What would change this answer

- If a 2024 PDG passage elsewhere stated "≥ 1 EeV" or "1 EeV and above" for UHECRs — none was found in the chapter; the verdict would flip to inclusive.
- If the requester intended Sec. 36 (non-accelerator detectors) — the value would become 10^17 eV, still exclusive.
- If the requester intended the Auger/TA community convention of 10^19 eV — that convention is *not* what the 2024 PDG cosmic-ray review states, and adopting it would misreport the source.

*Draft for review by a qualified scientist before citation or publication. All quotations are verbatim from the cited PDF build; the sha256 prefixes are those recorded at fetch time and should be re-verified against the live file before this is used in print.*

quotes.whole:
Earth’s atmospheric pressure varies with altitude as well, but Mars has a seasonal variation in pressure that does not occur here on Earth. It happens on Mars because the amount of CO2 gas in the atmosphere changes with the seasons. The Highest pressures occur during the southern summer months and the lowest pressures occur in northern summer months. What drives this change are different temperatures during northern and southern polar winters. Northern polar winters are relatively warm and short; the southern ones are long and severe.
The deep cold southern polar winter removes CO2 gas from the atmosphere by freezing it directly onto the south polar cap. As temperatures drop below –123° Celsius (–189° Fahrenheit), CO2 freezes out as frost, snow, or ice. This causes air pressure all over Mars to drop by 25% to 30%. Another way to understand this is that atmospheric pressure changes as the top layer of one polar cap migrates to the opposite polar cap in the form of air — and then migrates back half a Mars year later.

quotes.whole:
The circulation of Mars' atmosphere is simpler than Earth's, mostly because it has no oceans. At low latitudes, Hadley cell motion dominates. Named for English scientists George Hadley (1685-1768), who first described it on Earth, the pattern features rising, heated air around the equator. One part of the warmed air flows northward (and one part southward) to about 30° latitude (north and south), where it cools, sinks, and then flows back toward the equator at the surface.
The flow is prevented from moving directly north-south by the planet's rotation and the surface landforms, which direct the flow locally. In the northern hemisphere these surface winds blow generally from the northeast and in the southern, from the southeast.
At higher latitudes, polar air masses dominate and a series of high and low pressure areas sweep around the planet from west to east. Where these interact with Hadley cell movements, sharp weather fronts and even storms can arise. Martian frontal storms, however, tend to be less violent than terrestrial ones because the atmosphere is much thinner, temperatures are lower, and water vapor — which carries a lot of energy — is very minimal.

quotes.whole:
Mars has no ozone layer in its atmosphere as Earth does. This means ultraviolet radiation from the Sun and astronomical sources reaches the surface unhindered. This radiation is harmful for any exposed organic compounds. The lack of an ozone layer also means that the Martian atmosphere has no warm layer corresponding to Earth's stratosphere.
In addition to dust storms, Mars has clouds made of both water ice and CO2 ice particles. Scientists have studied these from orbit with spacecraft, from the ground with rovers and landers, and from Earth with big telescopes. Clouds collect near the large volcanoes as winds rise over them and ice particles condense. In winter, clouds also form over the polar regions as broad hazes that scientists call polar hoods.
The Phoenix lander, which touched down at latitude 68° north, detected CO2 snow falling from clouds passing overhead. The snow sublimated before reaching the ground. Other landers and rovers have detected water-ice frost on the ground on cold mornings. The frost disappears quickly after the Sun rises.

TECHNICAL MEMORANDUM
MARS GLOBAL REFERENCE ATMOSPHERIC MODEL (MARS-GRAM) 2024: USER GUIDE
1. INTRODUCTION
1.1 Background and Overview
Engineers and mission planners designing vehicles that pass through Mars’ atmosphere
require an atmospheric model that calculates the mean values and variations of atmospheric
properties. The Mars Global Reference Atmospheric Model (Mars-GRAM) is an engineering-oriented model that provides this critical information based on data tables derived from output
results from the NASA Ames Mars General Circulation Model (MGCM)1,2 and the University of
Michigan Mars Thermospheric General Circulation Model (MTGCM).3,4 Mars-GRAM is designed
to offer mission planners the flexibility to select input parameters such as time, latitude,
longitude, and dust level. Mars-GRAM outputs mean values for atmospheric density,
temperature, pressure, winds, and constituents along a user defined path. Mars-GRAM also
provides winds and density dispersions.

(MGS),5 Mars Odyssey (ODY), Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), and the Mars Atmosphere

verdict.summary:
RETRIEVAL RECORD AND VALUES FROM THE NASA MARS FACT SHEET (draft for qualified-scientist review; nothing here has been run or published)

1. SOURCE AND VERSION CONTROL
- Document: 'Mars Fact Sheet', NASA NSSDCA, author/curator Dr. David R. Williams.
- URL: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/marsfact.html
- Page's own version stamp (verbatim, footer): 'Last Updated: 19 May 2025, DRW'.
- Copy read: fetched 2026-11-22T23:29:31Z, content hash sha256 366b0ce9b69c... (hash as recorded by the fetch harness, truncated at 12 hex characters in the retrieved record).
- Why a 2026-11-22 fetch answers the 'as available on 2026-11-21' ask: the document's own last-updated date (19 May 2025) precedes both dates, so the same document version was being served on 2026-11-21 and on 2026-11-22; the one-day offset does not change the content. The site index page (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/) separately shows 'Last Updated: 13 November 2026, SAM', but that stamp belongs to the index page, not to marsfact.html, and must not be attributed to the fact sheet.
- Residual, non-blocking reproducibility caveat: an independent Wayback/archive snapshot dated exactly 2026-11-21 was not verified in this pass. If the reviewer requires a snapshot-pinned citation, pin the sha256 above against an archive capture before the draft is finalised.

2. ASK 1 - SURFACE PRESSURE AT MEAN RADIUS
Verbatim, from the 'Martian Atmosphere' block of marsfact.html:
  'Surface pressure:  6.36 mb at mean radius (variable from 4.0 to 8.7 mb depending on season)'
- Value as stated: 6.36 mb (the fact sheet writes 'mb'; 1 mb = 1 mbar).
- Unit conversion (using the fact sheet's own notes: 'Bar - ... 1 bar = 10^5 Pascal (Pa)' and 'millibars (mb = 10^-3 bar)', so 1 mb = 100 Pa): 6.36 mb = 6.36 x 10^-3 bar = 636 Pa = 6.36 hPa. The conversion is exact by definition, so the 3 significant figures of the source are preserved (636 Pa, not 640 Pa).
- Reference level: the fact sheet says 'at mean radius' and, in its bulk-parameter table, lists 'Volumetric mean radius (km) 3389.5', defined in the notes as 'Radius of a sphere with the same volume as the body'. So the 6.36 mb datum is referenced to the volumetric mean radius, 3389.5 km; it is not a value for a specific landing site and no areoid offset is stated on the page.
- Uncertainty: none stated. The fact sheet attaches no +/- value, error bar or confidence interval to 6.36 mb. Do not invent one; if the model needs an uncertainty distribution, that is a separate, explicitly documented assumption outside this retrieval.
- Sample size: not applicable / not stated - this is a single tabulated planetary value, not a sample statistic; the page gives no number of observations, instrument or mission attribution for this figure.

3. ASK 2 - SEASONAL RANGE
Same line, verbatim parenthetical: '(variable from 4.0 to 8.7 mb depending on season)'
- Value as stated: 4.0 to 8.7 mb.
- Unit conversion: 4.0 mb = 400 Pa (4.0 x 10^2 Pa, 2 significant figures as given); 8.7 mb = 870 Pa (2 significant figures).
- Consistency check against ask 1: the stated mean, 6.36 mb, lies inside 4.0-8.7 mb; the midpoint of the range is 6.35 mb, so the quoted mean is essentially centred (spread above the mean +2.34 mb, below the mean -2.36 mb; asymmetry 0.02 mb, i.e. below the rounding resolution of the endpoints).
- Interpretation caution: this is a seasonal variability envelope, not a measurement uncertainty on 6.36 mb. The fact sheet does not state which Mars years, which dataset, or which mission(s) the 4.0-8.7 mb envelope derives from, and it gives no n.
- Distinct figure that must not be confused with ask 2: the same line carries a second, site-specific range in square brackets, '6.9 mb to 9 mb (Viking 1 Lander site)' (= 690 Pa to 900 Pa). That is a lander-site range, not the global seasonal range, and is reported separately here.

4. VALUES TABLE (for direct transcription into the model input)
| Quantity | As stated by source | Unit (source) | Converted | Uncertainty | n |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Surface pressure at mean radius | 6.36 | mb (mbar) | 636 Pa / 6.36 hPa | not stated | n/a (single tabulated value) |
| Seasonal range | 4.0 to 8.7 | mb (mbar) | 400 to 870 Pa | not stated (envelope, not error) | not stated |
| Viking 1 Lander site range (separate, contextual) | 6.9 to 9 | mb (mbar) | 690 to 900 Pa | not stated | not stated |
| Reference datum: volumetric mean radius | 3389.5 | km | 3.3895 x 10^6 m | not stated | n/a |

5. INTERNAL CONSISTENCY CHECK ON THE SOURCE (flagged for the reviewer)
The site's summary 'Planetary Fact Sheet - Metric' table lists Mars 'Surface Pressure (bars) = 0.01'. That is 1000 Pa, 57% above the detailed fact sheet's 636 Pa, and 0.00636 bar does not round to 0.01 bar at any precision above one significant figure. Recommendation: take the model input from the detailed Mars fact sheet (6.36 mb / 636 Pa) and treat the summary-table 0.01 bar as a coarse entry, not as a second measurement. Do not average the two.

6. OUT OF SCOPE, CITED FOR CONTEXT ONLY (no modelling performed here)
- Elevation dependence: pressure on Mars also varies with elevation relative to the datum. Mars Education Program (Arizona State University), https://marsed.mars.asu.edu/mep/atmosphere (fetched 2026-11-22T23:29:32Z, sha256 09284b580d33...): 'the lowest place on Mars lies in the Hellas impact basin, 7.2 km ... below "sea level." The pressure there averages about 14 millibars.' A single mean-radius value therefore does not bound a landing-site pressure.
- CO2 seasonal cycle: same ASU page states the southern-polar winter freeze-out causes air pressure 'to drop by 25% to 30%'; the fact sheet's own 4.0-8.7 mb envelope is the tabulated expression of the same effect.
- Derived scale factor (approximation, derived here, not from the source): using the fact sheet's 'Scale height: 11.0 km' in an isothermal barometric relation, p(z) = p0 exp(-z/H) gives exp(-1/11.0) = 0.9131, i.e. ~8.7% pressure change per km of elevation at mean radius. This is a first-order engineering estimate only; for mission use the cited alternative is Mars-GRAM 2024 (NASA TM, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20240012934/downloads/Mars-GRAM%202024%20User%20Guide.pdf), which outputs 'Pressure at the zero altitude surface (Pa)' for user-specified time, latitude, longitude and dust level.
- Note on the fact sheet's provenance limits: the page gives no citation for the 6.36 mb or the 4.0-8.7 mb figures. If the model needs a primary reference, that must be sourced separately and is outside this request.

7. CITATION BLOCK FOR THE DRAFT
Williams, D. R., 'Mars Fact Sheet', NASA NSSDCA, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt MD. URL: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/marsfact.html. Page version: 'Last Updated: 19 May 2025, DRW'. Retrieved for this draft: 2026-11-22T23:29:31Z (content hash sha256 366b0ce9b69c...); content version identical to that available on the requested date 2026-11-21 by virtue of the 19 May 2025 last-updated stamp. Unit definitions from 'Notes on the Fact Sheets': https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/fact_notes.html (1 bar = 10^5 Pa; mb = 10^-3 bar).

8. STATUS OF THE TWO ASKS
Ask 1 answered: 6.36 mbar (636 Pa) at mean radius (3389.5 km), no stated uncertainty. Ask 2 answered: 4.0 to 8.7 mbar (400-870 Pa) depending on season, no stated uncertainty, no stated Mars-year or mission attribution. Neither ask is blocked. Every number above is quoted from, or converted by definition from, the cited page, with units, uncertainty status and sample-size status stated.

Earth’s atmospheric pressure varies with altitude as well, but Mars has a seasonal variation in pressure that does not occur here on Earth. It happens on Mars because the amount of CO2 gas in the atmosphere changes with the seasons. The Highest pressures occur during the southern summer months and the lowest pressures occur in northern summer months. What drives this change are different temperatures during northern and southern polar winters. Northern polar winters are relatively warm and short; the southern ones are long and severe.

The circulation of Mars' atmosphere is simpler than Earth's, mostly because it has no oceans. At low latitudes, Hadley cell motion dominates. Named for English scientists George Hadley (1685-1768), who first described it on Earth, the pattern features rising, heated air around the equator. One part of the warmed air flows northward (and one part southward) to about 30° latitude (north and south), where it cools, sinks, and then flows back toward the equator at the surface.

Mars has no ozone layer in its atmosphere as Earth does. This means ultraviolet radiation from the Sun and astronomical sources reaches the surface unhindered. This radiation is harmful for any exposed organic compounds. The lack of an ozone layer also means that the Martian atmosphere has no warm layer corresponding to Earth's stratosphere.

(or for the gas giants at the one bar level) in degrees C (Celsius or Centigrade) or degrees F
(Fahrenheit).  For Mercury and the Moon, for example, this is an average over the sunlit (very

changes on most of the planets.

pressures are not known.

moons are still being discovered.

obvious example.

quotes.whole:
Findings from NASA’s Juno probe released in October 2021 provide a fuller picture of what’s going on below those clouds. Data from Juno shows that Jupiter’s cyclones are warmer on top, with lower atmospheric densities, while they are colder at the bottom, with higher densities. Anticyclones, which rotate in the opposite direction, are colder at the top but warmer at the bottom.
The findings also indicate these storms are far taller than expected, with some extending 60 miles (100 kilometers) below the cloud tops and others, including the Great Red Spot, extending over 200 miles (350 kilometers). This surprising discovery demonstrates that the vortices cover regions beyond those where water condenses and clouds form, below the depth where sunlight warms the atmosphere.
The height and size of the Great Red Spot mean the concentration of atmospheric mass within the storm potentially could be detectable by instruments studying Jupiter’s gravity field. Two close Juno flybys over Jupiter’s most famous spot provided the opportunity to search for the storm’s gravity signature and complement the other results on its depth.

quotes.whole:
Juno’s data also shows that the belts and zones undergo a transition around 40 miles (65 kilometers) beneath Jupiter’s water clouds. At shallow depths, Jupiter’s belts are brighter in microwave light than the neighboring zones. But at deeper levels, below the water clouds, the opposite is true – which reveals a similarity to our oceans.
Polar Cyclones Juno previously discovered polygonal arrangements of giant cyclonic storms at both of Jupiter’s poles – eight arranged in an octagonal pattern in the north and five arranged in a pentagonal pattern in the south. Over time, mission scientists determined these atmospheric phenomena are extremely resilient, remaining in the same location.
Juno data also indicates that, like hurricanes on Earth, these cyclones want to move poleward, but cyclones located at the center of each pole push them back. This balance explains where the cyclones reside and the different numbers at each pole.

measurements of cloud movements over the past 20 years show
that, relative to the whole planet, Jupiter's zones have
strong winds, up to 320 kmph (200 mph).
On a rapidly-rotating planet .like Jupiter, planet-girdling winds on the edges of the zones, by definition
mean cross-zone temperature gradients. The reason is that
coriolis forces convert motions toward or away from the
poles into motions (winds) around the planet. As atmosphere
rises in the. zones and spills out the top in all directions,
its north and south notions are converted by coriolis forces
to flow" east and west.

the planet in alternating directions and at speeds at zone

JUPITER'S IONOSPHERE
The Pioneer data show that Jupiter's ionosphere has
at least five well-defined layers of differing electron
density, and there may be as many as seven layers. The
second layer from the top is especially pronounced, and may
have been produced by extreme solar ultraviolet radiation.
Jupiter's multilayered ionosphere rises more than
3,000 km (1,800 miles) above the one millibar pressure level
at the top of the planet's atmosphere. It is about five times
higher and five times hotter than had been predicted. The
ionosphere's unexpected depth is believed to be due to the
diffusion of its ionized gas by high temperatures. The
topside electron-ion temperature is about 600 degrees C.

verdict.summary:
SOURCE LOOKUP: JUPITER TEMPERATURES AT 1 bar AND 0.1 bar (NASA NSSDCA JUPITER FACT SHEET)
Draft for review — lookup and reporting only; no model was run.

1. SOURCE IDENTIFIED
Primary source: NASA NSSDCA 'Jupiter Fact Sheet', https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/jupiterfact.html (author/curator Dr. David R. Williams, NSSDCA, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center).
Retrieved: 2026-11-22T23:33:58Z by the harness; page sha256 9ac7835ae538.
Supporting source for definitions: 'Notes on the Fact Sheets', https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/planetfact_notes.html (retrieved 2026-11-22T23:33:58Z, sha256 88a8b66e5455).
Two other NASA pages were checked and rejected as the source of the requested numbers:
- https://science.nasa.gov/jupiter/jupiter-facts/ (page last updated Oct 15, 2026) — a public-facing feature page; the retrieved text contains no 1 bar or 0.1 bar temperature at all.
- https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/ (Planetary Fact Sheet – Metric, 'Last Updated: 13 November 2026, SAM') — lists a single column value for Jupiter, 'Mean Temperature (C) = -110'. Per the Notes page, that entry is defined as the average 'for the gas giants at the one bar level', i.e. it is the 1 bar value rounded to whole degrees C, not a 0.1 bar value. It is therefore not used to answer either ask, but it is a useful consistency check (see §5).

2. VERBATIM VALUES AS PRINTED (ask 1 and ask 3)
The 'Jovian Atmosphere' block of the Jupiter Fact Sheet reads, exactly:
  'Temperature at 1 bar: 165 K (-108 C)'
  'Temperature at 0.1 bar: 112 K (-161 C)'
Tabulated:
| Pressure level | Printed kelvin | Printed Celsius | Printed significant figures |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 bar   | 165 K | -108 C | 3 s.f. (K); 3 s.f. (C) |
| 0.1 bar | 112 K | -161 C | 3 s.f. (K); 3 s.f. (C) |
Note on typography: the page prints a bare 'C', not '°C'. Celsius values are quoted as printed; I do not restyle them.

3. DIRECT ANSWERS
- At 1 bar: 165 K, printed alongside -108 C.
- At 0.1 bar: 112 K, printed alongside -161 C.
Both Celsius figures are printed on the page. They are not derived by me for the answer; the derivation in §4 is a check only.

4. ARITHMETIC CHECK OF THE PRINTED CELSIUS VALUES (verification, not substitution)
Using °C = K - 273.15 (exact by definition of the kelvin scale, SI):
- 165 K - 273.15 = -108.15 °C → printed -108 C (rounded to the nearest whole degree; residual 0.15 K).
- 112 K - 273.15 = -161.15 °C → printed -161 C (rounded to the nearest whole degree; residual 0.15 K).
Both printed values are internally consistent with the printed kelvin values at the displayed precision. No discrepancy to report.

5. CROSS-CHECK AGAINST THE PLANETARY FACT TABLE
Planetary Fact Sheet – Metric gives Jupiter 'Mean Temperature (C) = -110'. The Notes page defines this quantity as the whole-planet average, 'or for the gas giants at the one bar level'. -110 C = 163.15 K, which is within 2 K of the 165 K printed on the Jupiter Fact Sheet — consistent given the differing rounding (whole-degree C vs whole-kelvin) and possible differing vintage of the two tables. This supports, and does not contradict, the 1 bar figure. There is no 0.1 bar entry anywhere in the planetary table.

6. UNITS, UNCERTAINTY, SAMPLE SIZE
- Units: kelvin (K) and degrees Celsius (C) as printed. Pressure levels in bar (1 bar = 10^5 Pa).
- Uncertainty: the Jupiter Fact Sheet prints NO uncertainty, error bar, or reference citation on either temperature value. The page does attach uncertainties to other quantities (e.g. atmospheric composition '89.8% (2.0%)'), so the absence here is a property of the source, not of the transcription. For a thermal model, treat 165 K and 112 K as nominal reference values with unspecified uncertainty; do not propagate them as if they had a stated error. If a numerical uncertainty is needed, it must be sourced elsewhere (e.g. a retrieved temperature profile) and stated explicitly.
- Sample size: n = 1 tabulated value per pressure level (a single published reference value, not a mean of a stated number of measurements). No averaging, no ensemble, no error of the mean is reported by the source.

7. VERSION / 'AS AVAILABLE ON 2026-11-21' (ask 2)
- The retrieved page (sha256 9ac7835ae538) was captured 2026-11-22T23:33:58Z, one day after the target date.
- The fact-sheet index page carries 'Last Updated: 13 November 2026, SAM', which precedes 2026-11-21.
- No revision marker dated between 2026-11-21 and the retrieval timestamp appears in the retrieved text of jupiterfact.html.
Conclusion: the quoted values are the ones the page carried on the target date to the best of the available grounding, but the one-day offset is a residual, documented risk. Recommended pre-publication step for the reviewer: confirm against an Internet Archive Wayback Machine snapshot nearest 2026-11-21 for the same URL and record its capture timestamp and hash alongside this table. If a snapshot differs, the snapshot's values supersede these and this draft must be revised.

8. WHAT THESE NUMBERS ARE (scope note for the thermal model)
- 'Temperature at 1 bar' is an atmospheric reference-level temperature, not a surface temperature. The same page states 'Surface Pressure: >>1000 bars', and the Notes page states that for the gas giants the surface is 'deep in the atmosphere and the location and pressures are not known'. Do not label 165 K as a surface temperature.
- The pair 165 K (1 bar) → 112 K (0.1 bar) implies temperature decreasing upward between these levels, i.e. the tropopause/stratosphere region of Jupiter. A simple thermal model must therefore not impose a single lapse rate through both levels; the two points bracket a temperature minimum region.
- No latitude, local time, or retrieval-geometry metadata accompanies either value; they are nominal global reference values.

9. LIMITATIONS TO STATE IN ANY DOWNSTREAM USE
(a) Single source, single value per level, no stated uncertainty. (b) One-day offset between target date and retrieval (see §7). (c) Celsius values are as printed at whole-degree precision; if the model needs sub-degree Celsius, convert from the kelvin values, not from the printed Celsius. (d) The fact sheet does not state which dataset or epoch these temperatures derive from.

Data from Juno shows that Jupiter’s cyclones are warmer on top, with lower atmospheric densities, while they are colder at the bottom, with higher densities. Anticyclones, which rotate in the opposite direction, are colder at the top but warmer at the bottom.

Juno’s data also shows that the belts and zones undergo a transition around 40 miles (65 kilometers) beneath Jupiter’s water clouds. At shallow depths, Jupiter’s belts are brighter in microwave light than the neighboring zones. But at deeper levels, below the water clouds, the opposite is true – which reveals a similarity to our oceans.

Jupiter has the shortest day in the solar system. One day on Jupiter takes 9.9 hours (the time it takes for Jupiter to rotate or spin around once), and Jupiter makes a complete orbit around the Sun (a year in Jovian time) in about 12 Earth years (4,333 Earth days).
With a radius of 43,440.7 miles (69,911 kilometers), Jupiter is 11 times wider than Earth. If Earth were the size of a grape, Jupiter would be about as big as a basketball.

Jupiter has 115 moons that are officially recognized by the International Astronomical Union. The four largest moons – Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto – were first observed by the astronomer Galileo Galilei in 1610 using an early version of the telescope. These four moons are known today as the Galilean satellites, and they're some of the most fascinating destinations in our solar system.
The Great Red Spot, a swirling oval of clouds twice as wide as Earth, has been observed on the giant planet for more than 300 years.

Juno data also indicates that, like hurricanes on Earth, these cyclones want to move poleward, but cyclones located at the center of each pole push them back. This balance explains where the cyclones reside and the different numbers at each pole.

quotes.whole:
For the base-ΛCDM cosmology, the cosmological parame-ters should have converged close to their true values by multi-poles ∼ 2000. Since ACTPol and SPTpol cover a much smaller
sky area than Planck the errors on their T E and EE spectra
are larger than those of Planck at low multipoles (see Fig. 10).
As a consequence, the current ACTPol and SPTpol polariza-tion constraints on the parameters of the base-ΛCDM cosmology
are much weaker than those derived from Planck. The ACTPol
results (Louis et al. 2017) are consistent with the Planck base-ΛCDM parameters and showed a small improvement in con-straints on extensions to the base cosmology that affect the
damping tail. Similar results were found by SPTpol, though
Henning et al. (2017) noted a >∼ 2σ tension with the base-ΛCDM model and found a trend for the parameters of the base-ΛCDM model to drift away from the Planck solution as the
SPTpol likelihood is extended to higher multipoles. To assess
these results we have performed some tests of the consistency of
the latest Planck results and the SPTpol spectra.
As a reference model for SPTpol we adopt the base-ΛCDM
parameters for the combined T E + EE fit to the SPTpol data

quotes.whole:
For the base-ΛCDM cosmology, the cosmological parame-ters should have converged close to their true values by multi-poles ∼2000. Since ACTPol and SPTpol cover a much smaller
sky area than Planck the errors on their T E and EE spectra
are larger than those of Planck at low multipoles (see Fig. 10).
As a consequence, the current ACTPol and SPTpol polariza-tion constraints on the parameters of the base-ΛCDM cosmology
are much weaker than those derived from Planck. The ACTPol
results (Louis et al. 2017) are consistent with the Planck base-ΛCDM parameters and showed a small improvement in con-straints on extensions to the base cosmology that affect the
damping tail. Similar results were found by SPTpol, though
Henning et al. (2018) noted a &2σ tension with the base-ΛCDM
model and found a trend for the parameters of the base-ΛCDM
model to drift away from the Planck solution as the SPTpol like-lihood is extended to higher multipoles. To assess these results
we have performed some tests of the consistency of the latest
Planck results and the SPTpol spectra.
As a reference model for SPTpol we adopt the base-ΛCDM
parameters for the combined T E + EE fit to the SPTpol data

verdict.summary:
ANSWER — Planck 2018 base-ΛCDM Hubble constant, as stated in the abstract

H0 = (67.4 ± 0.5) km s−1 Mpc−1  (68% confidence; base-ΛCDM; Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing)

This single line discharges all three asks: it is taken from the abstract of arXiv:1807.06209 (ask 1), it is the inferred Hubble constant (ask 2), and it carries both the uncertainty (± 0.5) and the unit (km s−1 Mpc−1) (ask 3).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. SOURCE AND SCOPE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Paper: Planck Collaboration VI (2020), "Planck 2018 results. VI. Cosmological parameters", arXiv:1807.06209 [astro-ph.CO]; published version A&A 641, A6 (doi:10.1051/0004-6361/201833910).
Scope: the abstract only, as the request specifies. Values appearing elsewhere in the paper are quoted below only as flagged context and are explicitly excluded from the answer.

Verbatim abstract sentence (the sentence from which the answer is read):

  "Assuming the base-ΛCDM cosmology, the inferred (model-dependent) late-Universe parameters are: Hubble constant H0 = (67.4 ± 0.5) km s−1 Mpc−1; matter density parameter Ωm = 0.315 ± 0.007; and matter fluctuation amplitude σ8 = 0.811 ± 0.006."

Version / rendering cross-check (this is the check that guards against an arXiv-version or typesetting artefact):
  - arXiv full text (ar5iv rendering of 1807.06209): reads "Hubble constant" followed by the same sentence, and separately the machine-readable line "H0 = (67.4 ± 0.5) km s−1 Mpc−1".
  - A&A published PDF (aa33910-18, the journal version of the same paper): identical sentence, identical digits.
  - Repository copy of the same A&A PDF (DTU Orbit portal file aa33910_18.pdf): identical sentence, identical digits.
  All three agree to the printed precision, so 67.4 ± 0.5 is not a rendering artefact of any single source. Any residual version risk is confined to arXiv v1/v2 pre-publication wording, which I did not retrieve; the published A&A text is authoritative and agrees with the current arXiv rendering.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. WHAT THE NUMBER IS — AND WHAT IT IS NOT
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
- It is a MODEL-DEPENDENT DERIVED parameter, in the authors' own words ("inferred (model-dependent) late-Universe parameters"). H0 is not a direct observable here; it follows from the measured acoustic scale (100θ* = 1.0411 ± 0.0003), Ωm and the assumption of a spatially flat 6-parameter ΛCDM cosmology with a power-law spectrum of adiabatic scalar perturbations ("base ΛCDM").
- It is a 68% MARGINALIZED CREDIBLE INTERVAL from the Planck posterior, not a frequentist standard error. The abstract states the convention explicitly: "in this abstract we quote 68% confidence regions on measured parameters and 95% on upper limits." The ± 0.5 is therefore a 68% interval; it must not be relabelled as 1σ, 95%, or "standard deviation" without saying so.
- SAMPLE SIZE: there is no N in the usual counting sense. The "sample" is the Planck 2018 legacy likelihood combination TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing fitted with 6 free parameters. This should be stated in place of an N whenever the number is quoted in a table alongside counting experiments.
- PRECISION: the abstract prints one decimal place. Quote (67.4 ± 0.5) km s−1 Mpc−1; do not append digits from elsewhere in the paper (see §3).
- Derived conveniences (clearly marked as derived, not printed):
    h ≡ H0/(100 km s−1 Mpc−1) = 0.674 ± 0.005  (dimensionless; uncertainty 0.5/100).
    Hubble time 1/H0 = 977.8 Gyr / (H0/100) = 977.8/67.4 = 14.51 Gyr; relative error 0.5/67.4 = 0.74%, so ±0.11 Gyr → 1/H0 = 14.5 ± 0.1 Gyr.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. UNCERTAINTY CONVENTION AND EXCLUDED VALUES
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Uncertainty as printed: ± 0.5 km s−1 Mpc−1 at 68% confidence. Fractional precision 0.5/67.4 = 0.74%.
If a 95% interval is required by a downstream table, a Gaussian approximation gives ±1.96 × 0.5 ≈ ±1.0, i.e. 67.4 ± 1.0 km s−1 Mpc−1 — label this as a DERIVED conversion, not as the printed number, because the posterior need not be exactly Gaussian.

Explicitly EXCLUDED from the answer (all are different quantities, different data combinations, or different locations in the paper):
  - Eq. (14) of the body: H0 = (67.36 ± 0.54) km s−1 Mpc−1 (68%, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing), described in the text as "our 'best estimate' of H0 from Planck". It is consistent with the abstract value (difference 0.04 km s−1 Mpc−1, well inside the ± 0.5 uncertainty) and its 0.54/67.36 = 0.80% precision matches the paper's own phrase "sharpens the determination of H0 to a 0.8% constraint". It is NOT the abstract value and is not reported as the answer.
  - Other H0 values that appear in the body for other combinations or as external comparisons (e.g. 67.9 ± 0.8 km s−1 Mpc−1 for a further combination; 73.3 +1.7/−1.8 km s−1 Mpc−1 attributed to Wong et al. 2019, an external measurement quoted for comparison). None appear in the abstract; none are used.
  - The abstract's BAO-combination clause ("Combining with baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) measurements (and ...") is truncated in the retrieved text and its H0 is a different data combination in any case; no number is inferred from it here rather than guessing.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. TRACEABILITY TABLE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Claim | Value | Source (retrieved) | Check
H0, base-ΛCDM, abstract | (67.4 ± 0.5) km s−1 Mpc−1 | arXiv:1807.06209 abstract (ar5iv rendering, sha256 cf434d51f10d); A&A PDF aa33910-18 (sha256 81553f594b16); repository copy (sha256 80a0dd9bf574) | identical digits in all three renderings
Confidence level of ±0.5 | 68% | same abstract: "we quote 68% confidence regions on measured parameters" | convention stated in the abstract itself
Model assumption | base ΛCDM = spatially flat, 6 parameters, power-law adiabatic scalar spectrum | same abstract | wording "Assuming the base-ΛCDM cosmology"
Context value (excluded) | (67.36 ± 0.54) km s−1 Mpc−1 | body, Eq. (14), A&A PDF | consistent with abstract to 0.04; 0.54/67.36 = 0.80% matches text's "0.8%"

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. HOW TO QUOTE IT (copy-ready)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Full: "Assuming the base-ΛCDM cosmology, the Planck 2018 abstract infers a Hubble constant H0 = (67.4 ± 0.5) km s−1 Mpc−1 (68% confidence; Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing)."
Short: "H0 = 67.4 ± 0.5 km s−1 Mpc−1 (Planck 2018, base ΛCDM, 68%)."

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. REVIEW CHECKS BEFORE THIS IS USED OR PUBLISHED
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. String match: confirm the character sequence "67.4 ± 0.5" appears in the abstract of the exact arXiv version being cited. If a version is found whose abstract differs, replace the value; this is the single falsifier for the entry.
2. Confirm the ± 0.5 is presented as 68%, not 95% — the abstract's own convention sentence is the authority.
3. Confirm the answer is not silently replaced by the body's Eq. (14) value (67.36 ± 0.54) when the question is about the abstract.
4. If the number is used in a comparison with local H0 measurements, retain the authors' caveat that the value is model-dependent and inferred, not directly measured.

STATUS: draft for review by a qualified scientist; nothing here has been run, and no data analysis was performed — the number is quoted, not derived.
